To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the erosion of theophylline matrix tablets containing 85% drug load is controlled by a mechanism of diffusion of theophyllin through the pores and cracks formed during the erosion of the matrix and that this diffusion process is affected by the compaction force and the presence of magnesium stearate and talc.
the erosion mechanism of a high drug‐load matrix tablet is dependent on lubricant type, lubricant concentration, compaction rate and porosity.
the erosion rate of high drug‐load theophylline matrices is a complex function of tablet porosity, lubricant type, and the compaction force applied.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and development of a novel extended‐release theophyl line formulation which has a high drug load (85%) to provide a controlled‐release dosage form for the management of asthma.
the development of a controlled release matrix formulation of theophylline for use in an extended release tablet.
the development of a new generation of extended‐release tablets with a high drug load (85% w/w) for use in the treatment of asthma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the drug release mechanism is a complex process involving both erosion and diffusion.
the drug release mechanism is a complex one, and that the release of theophylline is controlled by the erosion rate of the tablet.
the erosion of these high drug‐load tablets was a complex process, which was influenced by the amount of the lubricants, compaction rate and the porosity of the tablets.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the erosion mechanism was not affected by the presence of the lubricants, the compaction rate or the porosity of the tablets.
the erosion mechanism is the predominant mechanism for drug release from the high‐drug‐load tablets.
the erosion of the matrix tablets is the rate‐limiting factor for the release of theophylline.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a high drug‐loading in a matrix formulation is a viable option for achieving extended‐release.
the drug release rate from the tablets is dependent on the erosion rate, which is in turn dependent on the lubrication and the tablet porosity.
the drug‐load in the tablet is the primary determinant of erosion rate.
